opus-5.5.text:
I think if you go back a few years, the honest answer is that the amount of data would have been almost unimaginable, and that's partly why nobody really tried it seriously.

The traditional way to get a robot to do something like playing ball with a person was to collect demonstrations for that exact task. You'd teleoperate the robot, record the trajectories, and train a policy on them. The problem is that playing ball isn't one skill. You have to perceive a fast-moving object, predict where it's going, coordinate your whole body, and react to a human who isn't predictable. Every throw is a little different: different speed, different angle, different lighting, a different person with a different style. To cover all of that with task-specific demonstrations, you'd need an enormous number of episodes, probably orders of magnitude more than any lab could realistically collect. And even then the policy would be brittle. Move it to a new room or a new person and performance drops.

So in the older paradigm the data requirement scaled with the number of situations you wanted to handle, and for an interactive, dynamic task like this, the space of situations is huge.

What has changed is that we no longer think of the robot as learning everything from robot data alone. If you have a model that has already learned a lot about the physical world, how objects move, how people move, what a throw looks like, from large amounts of video and other data, then the robot-specific data only has to teach it the last mile. It has to connect that understanding to its own body and actions. That last mile is much smaller. Instead of needing data that covers every possible throw, you need enough to align the model's general physical intuition with control.

So I'd frame it this way. Earlier, the data cost was roughly "collect the whole world for this one task." Now it's closer to "learn the world once, then pay a much smaller cost per task." That shift is what makes something like playing ball with a person go from a research fantasy to something you can actually demonstrate.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier approaches would need an enormous amount of data and remain brittle, but does not suggest that no amount of data could enable the task.

r002.rationale: It centers the challenge on covering the many variations in throws, people, and settings, and explains that task-specific data would need to span that large situation space.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because it gets at the core of why robotics was stuck for so long.

If you think about an earlier model learning to play ball with a person, the way we approached it was essentially to teach the policy everything from scratch. The model doesn't know what a ball is. It doesn't know that a ball falls under gravity, that it bounces, that a person's arm swinging back means a throw is coming. All of that physical common sense has to be learned from data. And the only data that counts, in that paradigm, is robot data: the robot's own observations paired with its own actions.

So the amount of data you need is huge, and it scales with the diversity of the situation. The ball can come at different speeds, different angles, different lighting, a different person throwing it, a different room. Every one of those variations has to be covered in the training distribution, because the model has no prior to fall back on. In practice, people would collect tens or hundreds of thousands of teleoperation episodes, or run massive simulation farms, just to get a single task to work reasonably well. And even then, if you moved the robot to a new room, performance often collapsed.

The comparison I always make is to a child. A child doesn't need a hundred thousand throws to learn to catch. A few dozen attempts and they get the hang of it, because they already understand the world: objects persist, things fall, people have intentions. The learning of the skill itself is actually small. What's large is the understanding underneath it.

So when I think about the data earlier models needed, I think the number itself is almost the wrong thing to focus on. The real issue is that we were asking the robot data to carry the burden of teaching world knowledge, and robot data is the most expensive data there is. That's an inefficient split. The direction that makes more sense, and the one we've been pushing on, is to get the physical and semantic understanding from sources that are cheap and abundant, like video and language, and then let the robot-specific data be responsible only for the last mile: how this body, with these joints and this latency, actually executes the catch.

Once you do that, the data requirement for a task like playing ball drops dramatically. Not to zero, but to something that looks a lot more like a few hours of demonstrations rather than months of collection.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier systems needed huge amounts of data and could still fail in a new room, but it does not suggest that no amount of data could enable the task.

r002.rationale: It mentions variation in throws and the need to cover diverse situations, but identifies robot data carrying the burden of world knowledge as the central issue—not whether the model can cover the randomness of playing ball.

astra-6.text: I think earlier models would have needed a huge amount of data. Even something that looks simple, like playing ball with a person, involves recognizing where the ball is, predicting its trajectory, and coordinating your movements in real time. And the person can throw it at different speeds, from different angles. If the model mainly learns from examples, you have to cover all those variations. The question is whether it can learn something general about motion and interaction, so it doesn’t need to experience every possible throw before it can respond.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier models would need a huge amount of data, but does not suggest that no amount of data could have enabled the robot to play ball.

r002.rationale: It highlights the central challenge of covering different throws and asks whether the model can generalize without experiencing every possible throw.

sol-6.1.text: I think earlier models would have needed a lot of data, especially if you wanted the robot to play with different people in different environments. It’s not enough to learn one trajectory. The robot has to perceive the ball, anticipate where it’s going, and coordinate its movement in real time. And when it misses, it has to recover. If you’re trying to learn all of that from demonstrations, collecting enough examples becomes very expensive. So the question is how much of that behavior the model can generalize from what it has already learned, and how much requires new robot data.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier models would have needed a lot of data and that collecting examples would be expensive; it does not suggest that no amount of data would enable them to play ball with a person.

r002.rationale: The response frames the question as how much behavior can generalize versus how much requires new robot data. It does not identify covering the randomness of playing ball as the central question.
